J/ψ particles that decay into γ rays and undetected matter or energy, in addition to electrons or muons, can provide valuable insights for neutrino and dark energy research. By utilizing the BMV framework, which connects J/ψ invisible decays to neutrinoless double beta decay and dark matter decay, we establish a correlation between the decay rate of J/ψ into invisible matter/energy and neutrinoless double beta decay or dark matter decay. This connection holds across various energy scales and is unaffected by the dominant J/ψ decay modes. Consequently, a precise measurement of J/ψ invisible decays would yield a lower bound on the neutrinoless double beta decay rate or the dark matter decay rate. Furthermore, this research demonstrates that the significance of J/ψ invisible decays, particularly for light neutrino types (νe, νμ, ντ), is enhanced at higher energy levels, with a notable increase in importance at ΛQCD (10^43 GeV^2).

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) in two distinct dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA) and functional singular spectrum analysis (FSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework for the method's background, implementation, and a detailed explanation of our results. Notably, we conduct MFSSA in two separate time series domains, discovering that the spectrum obtained can be jointly interpreted to reveal coherent patterns across both domains. Conversely, isolating the analysis to a single domain yields less revealing spectral results. Our approach serves as a starting point for more intricate applications, such as using MFSSA in combination with other methods. We make available the multivariate functional singular spectrum examination toolbox, which includes implementation details and example use cases.

The long-term behavior of a random walk is significantly influenced by its initial starting point. For one-dimensional walks, either confined to one side of a barrier or restricted between two barriers, we examine the random process formed by the duration spent inside a specified zone, relative to its total time spent walking. A key aspect of this analysis is establishing the likelihood that future time spent within the designated zone will be substantial, regardless of the current time spent within that zone. A threshold can be identified where future time spent in the designated zone becomes more likely to be considerable than the current time spent in that zone. For walk durations bounded by two barriers, this threshold varies with the distance from the shorter barrier, while walks confined to one side of a barrier will exhibit a constant threshold. The probability of being beyond this threshold is maximal when the walk is even-handed, with a supermartingale approach used to derive this finding. The relevance of this finding to related problems, such as the likelihood of crossing a certain line within a specified time frame or the distribution of time spent within a designated zone, is also explored.

The IShTAR plasma source, a large-scale helicon, is evaluated for its performance in the helicon regime of operation. A review of plasma physics is followed by an examination of the source's design, focusing on the helicon region. A mathematical model previously developed for a similar source can be applied to IShTAR, and matching results from this model and experimental data have been found possible for both a small, locally tested version of the source and the full-sized IShTAR device. The mathematical model indicates that the source's operation is confined to the helicon regime.

Nucleus detection in histopathology images is a manually time-consuming task for pathology diagnosis, prompting researchers to use advanced technologies, including artificial neural networks. A crucial step in analyzing these images involves identifying specific types of nuclei, which can be automated through a category-aware nucleus detection process. To address this challenge, a novel two-stage W-Net is proposed, combining a lightweight U-Net for an initial prediction and a fully convolutional U-Net for refinement. The network is trained to categorize detected nuclei based on provided annotation data. Experimentation on two separate datasets shows the proposed method outperforms existing techniques in terms of F-score, accuracy, and loss, with results indicating it can be effectively applied to various medical field tasks.

Building on the principles established by Serre, we prove a regional converse theorem for specific instances of non-Archimedean L-functions, namely those associated with GL3(n) when n is odd and PSp6(2^k). These results hold under the assumption that the characteristic of the underlying field is greater than 3, does not divide n, and is not 2 for Sp6(2^k). Within this framework, we demonstrate that given a non-Archimedean L-function F, which is nearly self-dual and satisfies certain technical conditions, there exist isomorphisms between the adelic group A_F and specific subgroups of theadele groups associated with SO3(κ) when n is odd and Sps6(κ) when k > 1, provided that the conductor of F is sufficiently small in relation to the local ramification of the adelic group A_F.

In recent years, Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) have gained significant traction for solving complex data classification problems resulting from network analyses. However, the fundamental understanding of these networks as well as their individual component parts, especially the Graph Convolutional layer, remains limited among researchers. To address this knowledge gap, this study provides a detailed mathematical breakdown of the GCNN convolutional layer and offers a novel, in-depth analysis of the Heterogeneous Multi-Graph Convolutional layer, which includes derivations of its optimal weights and bias values. A thorough numerical investigation is also presented to compare our methodology to established GCNN training approaches, demonstrating the efficacy of our method in achieving precise solutions. A Python implementation of our methodology is made available through an open-source repository, enabling users to apply the methodology in real-world settings.

In a general theoretical framework, Einstein's theory of gravity is supplemented by a scalar field that is linked to it through a Chern-Simons action when applied to a specific, anisotropic, three-dimensional spacetime. This combination yields the scalar field's self-consistent equations, which are then shown to result in black holes and solitons that both rotate and possess hair, and these solutions are described in detail. The black hole's solutions are found to have specific properties, such as constant surface curvature, which can be either positive, negative, or zero, and the entropy of these solutions is demonstrated to be invariant across different parameters, thereby establishing a generalization of the famous Hawking's area law. The solutions also exhibit a periodic behavior as one of their parameters changes, which can be interpreted as a periodic, hairy black hole that returns to its original form after undergoing a cycle of growth, shrinkage, and re-growth induced by its own mass. This periodic behavior is an uncommon feature of black holes that are described by an equation known as the topological massive gravity theory. The solutions also interact with an externally applied, varying electromagnetic or Yang-Mills force, which causes them to become unstable before entering a complex, periodic phase of self-oscillation, and this oscillatory phase is found to influence the solutions' dimensions and spatial geometry. This oscillatory phase is also discovered to result in solutions with multiple, rotating, periodic black holes that are connected in a linked, ring-like structure

Elastography, an advanced imaging technique that highlights tissue texture based on tissue stiffness, is susceptible to inaccurate readings resulting from poor focusing due to significant displacement in soft tissues, especially in liver and breast imaging. To address this challenge, researchers have explored focusing methods such as synthetic aperture, delayed data acquisition, and virtual source techniques to improve the precision of elastography. In this study, a novel virtual origin synthetic aperture (VOSA) method is presented to enhance the accuracy of elastography in soft tissues by minimizing lateral displacement-induced focusing errors. Theoretical and experimental evaluations of VOSA demonstrated its effectiveness in precisely determining tissue stiffness with reduced error, even at significant displacement levels. In particular, the VOSA method showed its utility in accurately imaging stiff fibrotic liver tissue with minimal error, a key application in this research. In vitro and in vivo testing confirmed that the VOSA method could reliably detect soft tissue biomarkers in breast and liver imaging with high precision. In conclusion, the proposed VOSA method offers a cost-efficient solution to enhance the precision of elastography in imaging soft tissues with minimal displacement-induced focusing errors.

The growing availability of automated systems for perceiving and interpreting human interactions suggests a potential for similar automated analysis of written explanations.  To address this opportunity, we introduce a new framework that enables the automatic creation of efficient algorithms from informal descriptions.  We prove that any efficient algorithm can be effectively encoded as a system of constraints that, when solved, yields a comparable algorithm.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that efficient algorithms can be derived from certain types of demonstrations and streaming algorithms, respectively.  A high-level depiction of this process is illustrated in Figure 1.

The dynamic $k$-means clustering algorithm assigns data points to clusters based on their Euclidean distances to centroid representatives and allows for the addition or removal of points and centroids. This work focuses on the high-dimensional version of this problem, using a metric that reflects the intrinsic structure of high-dimensional data. We develop a two-step procedure for solving dynamic $k$-means in these situations. First, we create a distributional approximation to utilize the existing fast algorithms for solving large-scale mean estimation tasks. This approximation enables us to produce an efficient algorithm for clustering in response to data changes. Our approach guarantees an approximately optimal solution, with the quality of the solution dependent on the closeness of the data distribution to normality. To evaluate our method and compare it against existing approaches, we conducted experiments on real-world data sets covering a broad range of domains and found it outperforms these alternatives in most cases.

In a pioneering work, the authors have demonstrated a novel method for dividing a challenging pursuit-evasion game involving multiple agents with both deterministic and probabilistic movements. By creating a hierarchical framework, a large game with many uncertain elements can be efficiently solved by focusing on smaller, more manageable sub-domains. These sub-domains represent the optimal strategies for various state combinations and can be easily integrated to determine the overall winner or loser. A significant advantage of this hierarchical approach is the capability to maintain problem complexity despite incorporating extensive knowledge about the opponents. The proposed method is evaluated through simulations of a complex scenario featuring multiple pursuit agents and several evasive targets with varying levels of mobility.

At high-energy particle colliders, it is crucial to accurately measure the properties of vector bosons, particularly W and Z bosons, in experiments like future muon colliders and some leptonic scattering processes. However, due to the limited number of detected muons and their possible radiations, the traditional method of finding the parent particle location through neutrino missing momentum is not very efficient, with a significant loss of signal events and a large background increase. In this research, we introduce an alternative histological estimation method for the number and type of vector bosons based on detected muon characteristics, such as energy, angle, and radiation patterns, using machine learning and neural network techniques. By utilizing this method in leptonic W and Z boson scattering processes at a 1 TeV colliders, we find it possible to enhance the signal efficiency by 5 times and decrease the background by 10 times, allowing for precise property measurements of these vector bosons with a 0.5 TeV accuracy.

In complex environments, reinforcement learning tasks often share relevant information, and our proposed MBRM-Net excels at handling these co-existing tasks by addressing interference and identifying distinct state representations for better decision-making. Our innovative model enables efficient learning and adaptation to new tasks without requiring a reset of existing representations. Through rigorous testing, our method outperforms competing approaches in multiple challenging scenarios for multi-task learning, including the well-known Montezuma's Revenge.

This article discusses the progression of Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem, which led to the development of godel numbering, and ultimately resulted in the discovery of the fixed point theorem by Kurt Godel. Building upon this foundation, the authors demonstrate how the fixed point theorem can be applied to various formal systems, including primitive recursive arithmetic, first-order logic, and subsystems of arithmetic. By utilizing the fixed point theorem, the authors are able to derive a variety of significant outcomes, including the inconsistency of certain arithmetic theories, as well as the establishment of a fundamental distinction between computability and provability. The article also delves into the use of fixed point theorems within the context of programming languages and formal systems that incorporate the concept of truth. This study extends Hadamard's three spheres theorem to non-homogeneous second-order elliptic operators in Clifford analysis. Specifically, we prove that if $u$ is a non-constant function satisfying the operator equation, then the inequality $\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(B_1)} \leq \frac{C}{3} (\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(B_3)} - \|u\|_{L^{\infty}(B_2)})$ holds, where $B_1, B_2, B_3$ are concentric balls with radii $1, 2, 3$ respectively.

InInverse Issues represents a list of equations that need to be solved to extract valuable information from measurements, which are typically noisy, and are commonly encountered in scientific and engineering problems. A key aspect of Inverse Problems is posterior extraction, where the desired information is obtained from the generated measurement model, considering the noisy measurement as a conditional distribution. Although several methods have been proposed for this task, the measurement noise often encountered in real-world applications hinders the performance of these methods. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework based on a regularized conditional GAN, which enhances the measurement model by reducing the impact of noisy data. A key benefit of this proposed method is that it bypasses the computation of the posterior distribution, making it suitable for large-scale and time-dependent Inverse Issues. Experimental evaluations using synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method.

This study examines dynamical systems from Kyrgyzstan that feature multiple time delays. We establish that, under specific conditions, no long-term invariant surfaces exist beyond a particular critical point, given that two crucial parameters meet certain criteria. A novel method is employed to discover invariant surfaces, yet we find that surrounding the critical point, these surfaces suddenly cease to exist as the parameters shift, leading to the abrupt disappearance of these surfaces without evidence of hysteresis. A concise explanation for this sudden behavior is provided. Moreover, four distinct dynamic systems are presented as illustrative examples. These examples include nonlinear systems with both time delays and fractional-order components, as well as systems featuring multiple time delays, which are shown to exhibit complex, multi-stable patterns under certain conditions.

The interstellar medium is dynamic and affects how pulsars broadcast signals, particularly through scintillation patterns in pulsar brightness. By analyzing the spatial arrangement of these patterns, researchers can glean information about the medium surrounding pulsars, despite not having access to real-time data for most pulsars. This study utilizes archival observations of the bright pulsar PSR B1133+16, spanning 70 years and involving multiple scintillometry datasets from various radio frequencies, to investigate the variability of the medium surrounding this pulsar. It reveals a large-scale structure of the medium, attributed to a wall of high-velocity gas moving towards the Earth, and places this wall on a great circle in the sky. It also discovers a smaller, irregular pattern of scintillometry and infers that this pattern could result from a cloud of the wall's material that is moving transversely to Earth at high speed and is oriented parallel to the line of sight, allowing it to see the edge-on wall. This study further suggests that this wall surrounds the entire local bubble of the Milky Way and is moving towards the galaxy at a high velocity, likely as a result of a supernova explosion that emptied a neighboring star cluster, known as the Monoceros Ring, and is now drawing in its surrounding matter.

This paper introduces a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through a more efficient design. WN achieves realistic waveform generation using stacked autoregressive dilated convolution layers but struggles with large input sequences due to its sequential nature, leading to significant computational overhead. To address this challenge, a periodic neural network is proposed, with the aim of capturing recurring patterns in speech, using a design with relatively lower computational cost. This design is then combined with a non-linear and adaptive pitch control mechanism utilizing long short-term memory neural networks to regulate the model's pitch output. A two-path QPNet design is also explored for speech with distinct periodic characteristics in the low-frequency band, resulting in two separate models that are subsequently fused. Experimental evaluations using the LJSpeech dataset demonstrate the enhanced pitch control and lower computational overhead of QPNET compared to the standard WN design.

The bicategorical theory of shadows is a fundamental concept that serves as a basis for the bicategorical version of the Atiyah axioms in higher algebra. Bicategorical shadows can be thought of as a more advanced version of oriented bicategorical tracks, which in turn are equivalent to the bicategorical version of oriented cohomology. A key aspect of shadows is that they possess a well-defined degree, and this property plays a crucial role in the development of the Atiyah axioms. A significant finding of this research is that it demonstrates the bicategorical coherence of the Atiyah axioms in a general sense, and it also provides a more detailed understanding of the axioms' components, especially with regard to their degrees and how they interact with the fundamental bicategorical properties of shadows. A key feature of the axioms is that they can be expressed in a closed and self-contained manner using only shadows and their inherent properties, and this closed structure can be seen as a precise mirror image of the open and defining nature of the Atiyah axioms with respect to oriented cohomology. A useful tool in the study of the Atiyah axioms is the concept of oriented cohomology complex, and this research demonstrates the equivalence of the axioms to a specific, highly detailed description of the complex itself. For individuals who are deaf or hard-of-hearing, accessing auditory communication through vision is a difficult problem.  It requires the automatic identification of speech and other auditory objects in audio streams, followed by object localization in video streams that is independent of oral-gesture production.  This paper presents a novel approach to audio object localization in video streams that is applicable to individuals with whom one communicates through the visual-gesture-based language of hand signs.  It combines object detection in video streams utilizing a self-collaborative attention mechanism for better performance.  The model initially identifies potential objects, then employs a longitudinal approach to determine the active objects based on a longitudinal analysis of the video stream.  It also incorporates object detection in audio streams utilizing a sampling strategy with a self-reinforcement mechanism to enhance performance.  The model initially filters the audio features, then employs a self-reinforcement mechanism to detect auditory objects.  The proposed approach achieves superior performance on multiple datasets, also demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach for real-world applications.

Recently introduced as a novel neural network architecture, Lorentzian Neural Networks exhibit superior performance in comparison to their angular counterpart for specific tasks. Building upon this innovation, we present LGNNs, a pioneering study in our knowledge, which leverages Lorentzian neural networks to create a versatile node-level neural network for complex data processing. This work offers a comprehensive exploration of LGNNs through a representative dataset from the MIMIC-III dataset, demonstrating substantial gains in both training efficiency and accuracy in comparison to conventional graph neural networks.

This research aims to solve a problem that represents the dual scenario of a classic wave equation inversion, namely, given a source inside an enclosed space with which a flexible body is in contact, determine the source's movement from measurements of the surrounding air's vibration and the flexible body's vibration. A theoretical analysis is performed to demonstrate that, in a 2D setting with a specific type of contact, the source's movement can be recovered via a inverse problem that involves solving two connected partial differential equations. A computational method using a finite element method is then employed to numerically solve for the source's movement in a 2D scenario with an acoustic source inside an rectangular chamber filled with air and a flexible rectangular plate in contact with the chamber. A sensitivity analysis and the conjugate gradient method are used to recover the source's movement from numerical data. A study is conducted in which the source's movement, the shape and size of the chamber, and the shape and size of the plate are known, to recover the source's movement that corresponds to different types of sources, as well as an experimental approach using impact excitation. An algorithm that employs the method of fundamental solutions is also explored as an alternative computational method.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model that builds upon the fundamental principles of the Tsallis framework, incorporating an entropic parameter that influences the rate of discounting. This model offers a theoretical explanation for the observed asymmetry in delayed and premature decision-making consequences, as well as a framework for analyzing the relationship between the decision-making asymmetry parameter and the entropic index. A critical examination of the proposed model's implications provides insights into the potential outcomes of various decision-making strategies in a variety of contexts.

Building upon the harmonic gauge three-dimensional Einstein gravity model introduced in arXiv:2209.04567, we derive an identifying transformation that links the harmonic gauge to the de Donder gauge in this specific context. Notably, this relationship distinguishes itself from a well-known two-dimensional Einstein gravity scenario, where a similar transformation results in a translation of the conformal gauge field under a specific scaling. We demonstrate that the three-dimensional Einstein gravity harmonic gauge can be transformed into the Weyl conformally flat gauge, enabling us to solve a specific type of asymptotically flat spacetime near its singularity and provide a new formulation for the transformation that maps the harmonic gauge to the conformally flat Weyl gauge, utilizable in scenarios where the conformally flat Weyl gauge can be achieved.

Weyl-Wigner representations are used to state canonical classical mechanics equations and quantum thermodynamics equilibrium conditions in a phase-space formulation. A transformation is proposed to switch between two different Weyl-Wigner representation types, thereby offering a new perspective on a previously reported classical-to-quantum correspondence. This analysis also clarifies the proposed correspondence's original equation's solutions and provides a detailed examination of the representation transformation's implications for local operator averages. A connection to the proposed condition's original form is maintained through a change of variables, and the representation transformation's effects on average values of local operators are quantitatively assessed in both abstract and concrete, numerically computed examples.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has gone from a purely theoretical concept to a tangible reality in our laboratory environment. Since its initial proposal by Taub in 1954, the idea has been applied across various fields by different authors before being substantially proven in 1963 by Laxman-Manber for a specific type of quantum system, and later, in 1975, by Chiu for a more general scenario. Negative temperature was subsequently demonstrated in 1995 by Hahn for a specific type of atomic system and in 2000 by Budick for a general case using a two-level model. Additionally, researchers have explored its implications in physics, discovering connections to topics such as negative refraction, quantum entanglement, and cosmological theories.

In this analysis, we introduce an adjustable "scoto-seesaw" parameter $r$ to describe the relative sizes of light and heavy neutrino masses, which are determined by the ratio of their corresponding Yukawa couplings, i.e., $r = \frac{y_N}{y_{\nu}}$. We maintain the minimal assumption that the light neutrino mass arises from the spontaneous symmetry breaking of the scoto-seesaw framework. As a result, we derive the conditions under which the light neutrino mass falls within a specific range, potentially explaining the observed oscillation lengths. Furthermore, we examine the implications of this framework on dark matter phenomenology and Higgs vacuum stability in the $m_{\text{H}}(2m_{\text{W}})$ plane. We find that this model exhibits three distinct behaviors: (1) for very small $r$, it reduces to the minimal left-handed neutrino dark matter model, (2) for intermediate $r$, it results in our previous "inverse" dark matter scenario, and (3) for very large $r$, it leads to the "normal" minimal left-handed neutrino dark matter scenario. We also identify the regions in the $(m_{\text{N}}, r)$ plane that satisfy both dark matter relic density and Hubble expansion, and we analyze the effects of $r$ on the lightest dark matter neutrino mass and its implications for detection channels.

We employ a $sp^{3}d^{2}$ hybridization framework to describe the electronic structure of 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metal compounds, focusing on the overlap between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals. The proposed method allows for the direct calculation of band formations and their widths. The study reveals that the $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbital overlaps vary significantly with transition metal row, thereby influencing localizations of electrons. The resulting electron densities exhibit distinct patterns for each transition metal compound. The method is further adapted to model the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ blending in an orbital order-disorder scenario, mimicking the effects of temperature and strain. The research demonstrates how the proposed model can be utilized to simulate various phases and their associated transitions. The method has been applied to real materials like SrMoO$_3$ and MoSe$_3$, showcasing the proposed model's utility in modeling the band structures of these compounds. The method's effectiveness also extends to the simulation of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ blending in other, more complex materials, as demonstrated by simulations performed on perovskite and layered 4d and 5d transition metal compounds.

Building on related research by the authors and Jia, this study focuses on the interplay between relative quantum topological invariants and geometric characteristics in specific dimensions. It demonstrates the complexity of a specific type of singularities' invariants, using the example of hypersurface singularities from plane projections. Additionally, it establishes connections between the (graded) semi-positivity of Frobenius algebras, local birational transformations, and semi-positivity properties of Cohen-Macaulay graded modules. These relationships are examined through local and global analyses of planar arrangements, Kahler metrics on abstract convex cones, and complete intersections with divisorial contractions.

The classification of chest X-rays by artificial neural networks for identifying
lung conditions such as COVID-19 has been successful, but it has been observed
that these models are easily misled by simple transformations like flipping the
image, which contradicts a common assumption that these networks are invariant
to such reflections.  This issue might be more pronounced when it comes to
patient whose images have been altered due to conditions like emphysema.  This
work explores how sensitive modern classifiers are to lung conditions by creating
synthetic images that mimic real X-rays using emphysema as an example.  It is
found that these classifiers are sensitive to these conditions even after applying
simple transformations like flipping the image or rotating it by a few
degrees.  This suggests that even subtle changes in the lung structure could
confuse them.  This finding is particularly significant when it comes to models
based on deep learning that are being relied on heavily for medical decisions.
  These results raise important questions about relying on medical images that
have undergone significant alterations, as well as the need for more research
into creating more robust classifiers that can focus solely on the key features
of these images.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional vector data visualization and analysis. It allows users to create 2D visualizations of high-dimensional datasets via three different mapping approaches: classification, regression, and density estimation. With the application's interactive features, users can compare multiple visualizations simultaneously and switch between different visualization methods easily. It also features a point-in-space query tool, making it simple to examine target vectors within the context of the original dataset. ViDaExpert is a command-line tool that can be used directly or incorporated into larger scripts.
